paragraphs: Biclustering looks for groups in two related sets at the same time. This paper develops a framework that handles observations expressed as general labels, extending ideas from graph clustering to this broader setting. Its starting point is maximum likelihood: finding the grouping that best explains the observations under the model.

The authors then use a convex relaxation of that estimation problem. This supplies an optimization framework for recovering groups without directly solving the original formulation. A useful feature is that the same algorithm can also work effectively when only one of the two sets has cluster structure. That makes the approach relevant to some ordinary clustering problems as well.

The theoretical results give sufficient conditions for recovering the true clusters under a generalized stochastic block model. These conditions establish settings where recovery is supported; they do not say that recovery requires those conditions. Experiments on synthetic and real data provide further support for the framework and its recovery analysis.
icml-2015-a-convex-optimization-framewor.tldr: A convex framework handles clustering in one or two domains, with sufficient recovery conditions and supporting experiments.

paragraphs: Supervised metric learning uses labeled examples to learn how similarity should be measured. This paper asks how a metric learned elsewhere can help a new learning problem. Earlier empirical applications suggested that transferring such knowledge could be useful; the authors develop a theoretical justification for incorporating a source metric into regularized learning.

The source metric influences the regularizer, steering the learned metric toward prior knowledge. To analyze this procedure, the authors introduce an on-average-replace-two notion of algorithmic stability. This measures sensitivity to changes in training data in a way suited to their setting, and supports proofs of fast generalization rates when the auxiliary metric biases the regularizer.

A consistency result further motivates weighted formulations that control the influence of this bias. The paper also provides a way to estimate the associated weight, connecting the analysis to a practical modeling choice. Experiments illustrate the approach on standard metric learning tasks and on a transfer problem with few labeled examples.
icml-2015-a-theoretical-analysis-of-metr.tldr: A stability analysis supports using a source metric to guide regularized metric learning, including when labeled data are scarce.

paragraphs: Stochastic variational inference offers a way to make Bayesian inference practical on large datasets. Much of the evidence about how to use it effectively had come from topic models, especially latent Dirichlet allocation. This paper investigates whether the same lessons hold for beta process factor analysis, a model that represents observations through sparse latent factors.

The authors derive several inference algorithms and study them using synthetic, image, and genomic data. Their central question concerns posterior dependencies: relationships between unknown quantities after observing data. An approximation that treats these quantities separately can behave differently from one that preserves selected relationships, so the choice of dependencies matters to inference performance.

The experiments support a broad lesson from topic modeling: incorporating Gibbs sampling within stochastic variational inference can be extremely effective for maintaining useful dependencies. However, the dependencies that matter in beta process factor analysis differ from those important in latent Dirichlet allocation. The practical message is to preserve relationships appropriate to the particular model.
icml-2015-an-empirical-study-of-stochast.tldr: Experiments show that preserving posterior dependencies helps stochastic variational inference, but the useful dependencies depend on the model.

paragraphs: Local graph diffusion spreads information through a network to help rank vertices and identify nearby communities. Personalized PageRank and the heat kernel are two established choices. This paper develops an efficient local approximation algorithm for a diffusion that generalizes both, expanding the range of diffusion behaviors available for graph clustering.

The key mathematical step is to express the diffusion vector as the solution of an initial value problem. This describes how the diffusion develops from a specified starting state. The authors then apply waveform relaxation to approximate that solution, turning the mathematical formulation into a computational method for producing local graph rankings.

Experiments suggest that the resulting rankings are both distinct from and competitive with those produced by high-quality personalized PageRank and localized heat-kernel implementations. Distinct rankings matter because another diffusion can expose a different view of the same graph. The evidence supports the method as a useful addition to existing tools, without establishing that it consistently replaces either alternative.
icml-2015-community-detection-using-time.tldr: A local diffusion algorithm generalizes PageRank and the heat kernel, producing experimentally competitive but distinct graph rankings.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent improves a solution by updating one coordinate at a time, making the selection rule an important design choice. Earlier theory assigned the same convergence rate to random selection and the Gauss-Southwell rule, despite the latter typically costing more to apply. Experiments nevertheless often favored Gauss-Southwell when selection costs were comparable.

This paper gives an analysis showing a faster convergence rate for Gauss-Southwell except in extreme cases. It therefore helps explain the gap between the earlier theoretical comparison and observed behavior. The distinction between convergence rate and selection cost remains important: an improvement in the former does not by itself settle total computational expense.

The authors also show that exact coordinate optimization improves rates for certain sparse problems. A proposed Gauss-Southwell-Lipschitz rule achieves a further rate improvement when the partial derivatives' Lipschitz constants are known. Analyses of approximate selection rules and proximal-gradient variants extend the discussion to additional ways of implementing coordinate updates.
icml-2015-coordinate-descent-converges-f.tldr: A sharper analysis explains why Gauss-Southwell coordinate selection usually converges faster than random selection, while retaining computational-cost considerations.

paragraphs: Edge-aware image filters have many different mathematical forms and implementations, making a common acceleration strategy difficult. This paper learns an important family of these operators from data. Its goal is to approximate their behavior through a shared neural-network framework, so that different filtering effects can use the same computational approach.

The method uses a deep convolutional neural network trained in the gradient domain, focusing training on image changes represented by gradients. It can approximate filters without needing their original mathematical models or implementation details. Within this framework, the learned parameters distinguish one operator from another, allowing a common architecture to represent varied filtering behavior.

The authors report acceleration of up to 200 times for complex edge-aware filters. This is a reported maximum, rather than a speedup promised for every operator. The framework also achieves fast processing for effects built from spatially varying filters or combinations of filters, showing that its usefulness extends to composing new image effects.
icml-2015-deep-edge-aware-filters-256896.tldr: A shared convolutional network learns to approximate varied edge-aware filters, with reported acceleration of up to 200 times.

paragraphs: Training large neural networks can be constrained by the computing resources available. This paper studies whether training can use limited numerical precision while retaining classification performance. It examines both how numbers are represented and how computations are performed, concentrating on low-precision fixed-point arithmetic.

A central finding is that the rounding rule strongly affects training behavior. When arithmetic produces values that the chosen representation cannot express exactly, the way those values are rounded becomes part of the learning procedure. The authors find that stochastic rounding enables deep networks to train with 16-bit fixed-point numbers while showing little or no degradation in classification accuracy in their results.

The paper also demonstrates an energy-efficient hardware accelerator implementing this arithmetic and rounding combination. That connects the training experiments to a concrete computing design. The contribution is therefore both an empirical result about learning with restricted precision and a hardware demonstration of how the successful numerical approach can be implemented.
icml-2015-deep-learning-with-limited-num.tldr: Stochastic rounding enables 16-bit fixed-point neural-network training with little or no reported accuracy loss and supports an energy-efficient accelerator.

paragraphs: This paper develops a deep generative model that produces an independent sample in a single forward pass through a multilayer neural network. It shares this convenient sampling structure with generative adversarial networks. Its training approach addresses the difficulty of optimizing the adversarial minimax objective by using a statistical comparison between generated samples and data.

The comparison is maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD, a technique from statistical hypothesis testing. The resulting objective can be interpreted as matching statistics of all orders between the two sample collections and can be optimized by backpropagation. This gives the generator a direct training criterion based on how its output distribution differs from the observed data.

The authors further improve performance by combining the generator with an autoencoder. The generator learns to produce codes using MMD, and the decoder turns those codes into samples. Evaluations on MNIST and the Toronto Face Database report strong generative performance relative to the baseline approaches considered, supporting the combination of distribution matching and learned representations.
icml-2015-generative-moment-matching-net.tldr: Generative moment matching networks use MMD to train fast-sampling generators, with an autoencoder combination improving reported performance.

paragraphs: Some random quantities naturally lie on curved spaces, such as positions on a sphere or rotations. This paper addresses the shortage of flexible probability models for these spaces that are also easy and fast to train. It defines harmonic exponential families on manifolds including the torus, sphere, and rotation groups.

The computational contribution is an efficient way to calculate the gradient of the log-likelihood using a non-commutative generalization of the Fast Fourier Transform. Efficient gradients make fitting these distributions more practical. The approach connects the flexibility of the probability model with computation adapted to the structure of the space on which the data live.

The paper discusses Bayesian camera-motion estimation, where these distributions serve as conjugate priors, and modeling earthquake locations on Earth's surface. Its experiments report significantly higher likelihood than the best competing method while reducing training time by orders of magnitude. These results support the proposed combination of flexible densities and efficient fitting in the evaluated settings.
icml-2015-harmonic-exponential-families-.tldr: Harmonic exponential families model distributions on curved spaces using efficient Fourier-based training, with strong reported likelihood and speed results.

paragraphs: Hashing supports approximate nearest-neighbor search by learning representations suited to finding similar items. Many hashing methods assume all training data are available in one place. This paper tackles situations where data are stored or collected across machines and gathering them centrally would impose prohibitive communication and computation costs.

The authors reformulate a centralized hashing model as multiple subproblems linked by consensus constraints. Each compute node can solve its subproblem analytically and in parallel, while the constraints coordinate the distributed solutions. This makes distributed learning part of the optimization formulation rather than requiring the original data to be pooled before training begins.

No training data are transmitted between nodes during learning, and the model's communication cost is independent of dataset size. This claim concerns the communication design, rather than eliminating all distributed coordination. Experiments on several large datasets, including one scale of up to 100 million samples, demonstrate the method's effectiveness for learning hash functions in this distributed setting.
icml-2015-hashing-for-distributed-data-0.tldr: A consensus-based hashing model trains across machines without transmitting training data, making communication cost independent of dataset size.

paragraphs: Feature selection is commonly used in security applications to improve generalization and reduce computation. This paper asks whether those benefits remain reliable when an attacker can insert malicious examples into the training set. The concern is that poisoned data may influence which features a learning system decides to retain.

The authors provide a framework for investigating the robustness of methods including LASSO, ridge regression, and the elastic net. This makes feature learning itself an object of adversarial evaluation. Rather than assuming a preprocessing or regularization choice improves security, the approach examines how deliberately manipulated training data can compromise that choice.

In malware-detection experiments, the studied methods can be substantially affected. A particularly striking result is that carefully inserting less than five percent poisoned training samples makes LASSO's feature-set choices nearly random. This describes the selected features, rather than a stated classification-accuracy figure. The findings motivate specific countermeasures against poisoning instead of relying on feature selection alone for robustness.
icml-2015-is-feature-selection-secure-ag.tldr: Malware experiments show that carefully poisoned training data can severely compromise feature selection, including nearly randomizing LASSO's selected features.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process methods need efficient kernel computations to scale to large datasets. This paper introduces structured kernel interpolation, or SKI, as a framework that unifies and generalizes inducing-point approaches. It constructs kernel approximations through interpolation, providing a common way to understand existing methods and create new ones.

The framework makes explicit three influences on approximation quality: the number of interpolation points, the interpolation strategy, and the covariance kernel. Choosing local cubic interpolation yields KISS-GP. This method also enables structured Kronecker and Toeplitz computations for additional scalability gains without requiring the observed data themselves to lie on a grid.

The paper states that KISS-GP requires time and storage linear in the number of observations for Gaussian-process inference and is more scalable than inducing-point alternatives. It also supports fast, expressive kernel learning. Evaluations examine kernel-matrix approximation, kernel learning, and natural-sound modeling, connecting the computational framework to both approximation quality and learning useful covariance structure.
icml-2015-kernel-interpolation-for-scala.tldr: KISS-GP uses structured kernel interpolation for linear-time, linear-storage Gaussian-process inference without requiring grid-structured observations.

paragraphs: Dependent nonparametric trees model hierarchies that change over time without fixing the tree size in advance. Their flexibility comes with substantial computational demands. This paper develops a distributed training system that addresses both exploring possible tree structures and updating the model from very large datasets.

The inference method combines memoized variational inference with a birth-and-merge strategy for exploring the unbounded tree space. Model parallelism lets different parts of the tree grow or shrink concurrently, using conflict-free partitions and lightweight synchronization to maintain alignment. Data parallelism separately distributes variational parameter updates, so the system can process many observations across compute resources.

Using 64 cores for 36 hours, the system learns a topic tree with 10,000 nodes from eight million documents, capturing both common and long-tail topics. The reported data and model scales exceed recent hierarchical Dirichlet-process results by orders of magnitude. Near-linear scalability suggests potential for larger problems, although that potential is distinct from the demonstrated run.
icml-2015-large-scale-distributed-depend.tldr: Distributed inference makes evolving nonparametric topic trees practical at a demonstrated scale of eight million documents and 10,000 nodes.

paragraphs: Many prediction problems involve several outputs whose values are statistically related. This paper combines deep learning with Markov random fields, which encode dependencies among those outputs. The aim is to learn rich input representations while also accounting for how the predicted variables relate to one another.

The proposed training algorithm learns deep features and the structured model jointly. The features form the Markov random field's potentials, linking the learned representation directly to the quantities used for structured prediction. Its computational approach blends learning with inference and uses GPU acceleration, making the combined training procedure efficient.

The authors evaluate the algorithm on predicting words from noisy images and tagging Flickr photographs. They report significant performance gains from jointly learning deep features and Markov random field parameters. The result supports coordinating representation learning with output-dependency modeling: the features are trained as part of the same predictive system that uses relationships between outputs, rather than being treated as a separate fixed input.
icml-2015-learning-deep-structured-model.tldr: Jointly training deep features and Markov random fields improves reported performance on tasks with statistically related outputs.

paragraphs: When a system makes several predictions together, the cost of their combined errors may not decompose into separate costs for each prediction. This paper studies convex surrogate losses for such set-prediction problems. These surrogates provide optimization objectives for learning when the original loss depends on the collection of mistakes.

The authors show that margin and slack rescaling yield tight convex surrogates exactly when the underlying loss increases with the number of incorrect predictions. However, computing gradients or cutting planes for these constructions is NP-hard for non-supermodular losses. Thus, a favorable mathematical relationship to the original loss does not necessarily make training computationally tractable.

For submodular losses, the paper introduces the Lovasz hinge. Computing a gradient or cutting plane takes O(p log p) work and O(p) accesses to the loss function. The authors present it as the first tractable convex-surrogate construction for this class and demonstrate its utility on a real-world image-labeling task, connecting the optimization result to structured prediction.
icml-2015-learning-submodular-losses-wit.tldr: The Lovasz hinge provides a tractable convex surrogate for submodular prediction losses, avoiding a computational obstacle in standard rescaling approaches.

paragraphs: Standard long short-term memory models organize their memory along a chain. This paper extends that idea to trees, where a unit may need to combine information from several branches. The proposed S-LSTM lets a memory cell incorporate histories from multiple child cells or multiple descendants through recursive computation.

This structure offers a principled way to represent long-distance interactions within hierarchies, including language or image parse structures. The authors apply it to semantic composition: combining parts of text to understand its meaning. In that setting, the tree provides information about how pieces should be combined, while the memory blocks carry information through the hierarchy.

Replacing a state-of-the-art recursive model's composition layers with S-LSTM blocks improves performance in the reported study. The authors also find that using the supplied structures performs better than ignoring them. Together, these results support both the proposed memory mechanism and the value of structural information for the semantic-composition task evaluated.
icml-2015-long-short-term-memory-over-re.tldr: S-LSTM extends memory cells to trees and improves reported text-composition performance by using hierarchical structure.

paragraphs: Expensive black-box optimization becomes harder when the conditions defining an acceptable solution are also unknown. This paper examines problems with using expected improvement to choose evaluations in that setting. In particular, objective and constraint evaluations may be available independently, creating a need to decide which kind of information to acquire.

The authors describe two failure modes. With independently evaluated constraints, expected improvement can encounter a pathology that prevents exploration. It also requires a current best solution, which may be unavailable when no observed point satisfies the constraints. Information-based approaches avoid these particular difficulties because their evaluation criterion does not rely on the same improvement calculation.

The proposed method, Predictive Entropy Search with Constraints, applies this information-based perspective to constrained Bayesian optimization. Evaluations on synthetic problems, benchmarks, and real-world examples compare favorably with expected-improvement methods. The findings support PESC as an effective approach and a promising step toward a unified treatment of constrained optimization, rather than establishing a complete universal solution.
icml-2015-predictive-entropy-search-for-.tldr: PESC uses information-based evaluation to handle unknown constraints and avoid specific exploration failures of expected improvement.

paragraphs: Multi-armed bandit problems involve learning which choices produce desirable outcomes through repeated interaction. This paper considers a setting where outcomes can be ordered but are not numerical. Such qualitative rewards support comparisons, yet arithmetic operations such as averaging have no valid meaning, so the usual mean-based description of a choice is unavailable.

The authors use a quantile of each choice's reward distribution as its representative value. A quantile identifies a position within an ordered distribution, allowing the learning objective to respect the qualitative reward scale. This changes how choices are assessed while retaining the central challenge of learning about uncertain outcomes through experience.

The paper develops algorithms for two settings: a finite horizon devoted to pure exploration and an infinite horizon focused on cumulative regret minimization. It analyzes their properties and provides initial experiments illustrating them. The contribution is a formal framework and associated methods for online learning when reward order is meaningful but numerical averages are not.
icml-2015-qualitative-multi-armed-bandit.tldr: Quantile-based bandit algorithms enable online learning from rewards that can be ranked but cannot meaningfully be averaged.

paragraphs: Multi-task feature learning learns related tasks together, but extremely large feature sets make optimization costly. This paper proposes a screening rule based on dual projection onto convex sets, called DPC. It identifies features whose coefficients will be zero across every task in the solution.

The rule is safe: every feature it flags is guaranteed to be inactive in those solution vectors. Removing such features can therefore reduce computation and memory without sacrificing accuracy. The method applies to sparse models with multiple data matrices and has low computational overhead, allowing it to be incorporated into existing solvers.

Deriving the rule requires solving a nonconvex problem. The authors show that an appropriate parametrization of its constraint set makes the global optimum efficiently obtainable. Experiments on synthetic and real data show effective identification of inactive features, particularly in high-dimensional settings, with speedups reaching several orders of magnitude. Those gains reflect the benefit of shrinking the optimization problem before solving it.
icml-2015-safe-screening-for-multi-task-.tldr: DPC safely removes features guaranteed to be inactive across all tasks, producing substantial reported savings in multi-task learning.

paragraphs: This paper builds a topic model that uses a deep hierarchy to represent interactions among topics. Its foundation is Poisson factor analysis, with topics selected by binary variables in the bottom layer of a deeper graphical model. The hierarchy supplies a flexible prior that helps reveal structure in topic usage.

The deep component can be a sigmoid belief network or a restricted Boltzmann machine. Topics remain at the bottom of the overall model; the layers above them describe latent binary structure influencing their selection. This separates the topics themselves from the deeper mechanism that captures relationships among them.

To make learning scalable, the authors derive inference algorithms using Bayesian conditional density filtering and extensions of stochastic gradient thermostats. Experiments across several text corpora show that the approach handles very large document collections and learns structured topic representations. It also obtains better test perplexities than related models in those evaluations, supporting the usefulness of the deep prior for modeling unseen text.
icml-2015-scalable-deep-poisson-factor-a.tldr: Deep binary hierarchies guide topic selection in scalable Poisson factor analysis, improving reported test perplexity on several corpora.

paragraphs: Log-supermodular models can represent binary-variable dependencies, including interactions involving more than two variables. Those higher-order interactions create difficulties for existing approximate inference methods. This paper studies L-Field, a variational approach, and identifies a connection that makes its optimization substantially more efficient.

The authors show that the L-Field problem reduces to a minimum-norm problem associated with submodular minimization. Existing optimization tools can then solve it orders of magnitude faster than previously possible. They also prove that L-Field exactly minimizes a particular Renyi divergence, providing an interpretation of what its approximation is optimizing. Exact minimization of that divergence still describes a variational approximation.

The paper further develops parallel inference as message passing on a suitable factor graph, with a linear convergence rate and no need to sum over every factor configuration. An image-segmentation application demonstrates scalability, high-quality marginal estimates, and benefits from higher-order potentials. These findings link faster computation with the ability to use richer dependency models.
icml-2015-scalable-variational-inference.tldr: A minimum-norm reformulation accelerates L-Field inference and enables parallel message passing for models with higher-order interactions.

paragraphs: Sparse principal component analysis seeks a component involving only selected variables. This paper adds a structural requirement: the variables with nonzero entries must lie along a path in a supplied directed acyclic graph. The graph therefore determines which groups of variables are allowed to participate together in the extracted component.

The proposed estimator incorporates this information through a nonconvex quadratic maximization using the empirical covariance. The authors analyze a simple network under the spiked covariance model for sparse PCA. Their analysis shows that graph information can potentially reduce statistical complexity, meaning that suitable structural knowledge may lower the observations needed to recover the population component.

Because the optimization problem is nonconvex, the paper proposes two algorithms that approximate its solution while recovering a component with the required path structure. Evaluations use synthetic and real datasets. The contribution combines a structured estimator, a conditional statistical argument for using network information, and computational approaches for obtaining components that respect that information.
icml-2015-stay-on-path-pca-along-graph-p.tldr: Graph-path constraints guide sparse PCA and can potentially reduce the data needed to recover a principal component.

paragraphs: This paper trains deep convolutional networks to predict moves made by expert Go players. The motivation is to build playing strength through recognizing board patterns, given that strong computer Go programs commonly examine millions of future positions. Expert move prediction supplies the training task for learning useful patterns.

The authors introduce several techniques, including tying network weights to encode symmetries expected in the target function. An ablation study shows that the introduced techniques considerably improve performance. The final networks reach move-prediction accuracies of 41.1 percent and 44.4 percent on two datasets, exceeding the previous state of the art on that task.

The authors also evaluate actual playing ability, since accurately predicting expert moves does not automatically establish game-playing strength. Their networks consistently defeat GNU Go and win some games against Fuego while using a fraction of the play time. These results show that the learned predictors acquire substantial playing skill, with the reported strength against Fuego remaining qualified.
icml-2015-training-deep-convolutional-ne.tldr: Convolutional networks trained on expert Go moves achieve strong prediction results and substantial playing skill with comparatively little play time.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process-modulated Poisson processes model event occurrences using a flexible, uncertain event-rate function. They are useful in areas including neuroscience, geostatistics, and astronomy, but existing inference methods can be computationally expensive. This paper presents what the authors identify as the first fully variational Bayesian inference scheme for the continuous version of these processes.

The scheme works without discretizing the domain, so inference does not require replacing continuous space or time with a collection of bins. Its computational cost grows linearly with the number of observed events. The authors also report that it is many orders of magnitude faster than earlier sampling-based approaches, directly addressing a barrier to using these models.

Evaluations cover synthetic examples, coal-mining disaster data, and prediction of malaria incidences in Kenya. The resulting algorithm outperforms standard methods in those studies. Together, the continuous-domain formulation, favorable scaling, and reported application results support more practical Bayesian analysis of event data using this class of point-process models.
icml-2015-variational-inference-for-gaus.tldr: A fully variational method fits continuous Gaussian-process-modulated Poisson processes without discretization and scales linearly with observed events.

paragraphs: Bayes by Backprop learns a probability distribution over a neural network's weights. This makes uncertainty about the weights an explicit part of the learned model. The paper presents the algorithm as efficient, principled, and compatible with backpropagation, connecting probabilistic weight learning to the training machinery used for neural networks.

Training regularizes the weights by minimizing a compression cost expressed through variational free energy. The uncertainty representation therefore participates in the learning objective rather than being added only after training. On MNIST classification, the authors report performance comparable to dropout, showing that this form of regularization can be competitive in that evaluated setting.

The paper also demonstrates two uses of the learned uncertainty beyond classification regularization. It improves generalization in nonlinear regression problems and helps drive the exploration-exploitation trade-off in reinforcement learning. These examples show how uncertainty in model weights can contribute both to predictions on new data and to decisions about which actions to explore.
icml-2015-weight-uncertainty-in-neural-n.tldr: Bayes by Backprop learns uncertainty over neural-network weights for regularization, regression generalization, and reinforcement-learning exploration.
